print(np.round(values, 3))
hints: Recall the theoretical PACF signature of a pure AR(p) process: it cuts off sharply to (statistically) zero after lag p.
This is an AR(1) process, so p = 1 -- which single lag should carry essentially all of the PACF's nonzero signal?
The PACF value at lag 1 for an AR(1) process should land close to phi itself; lags 2, 3, and 4 should be close to zero, not decaying gradually the way the ACF would.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints roughly [1.0, 0.8, ~0.0, ~0.0, ~0.0] (lag 0 is always 1.0 by definition, lag 1 lands close to the true phi = 0.8, and lags 2 through 4 are close to zero, within sampling noise). This is the textbook AR(1) PACF signature: a single sharp spike at lag 1, then a cutoff to essentially zero, because once X_(t-1) is controlled for, none of the more distant lags add any further direct explanatory power.
exercises.solutionExplanation: For a pure AR(1) process, the theoretical PACF is exactly phi at lag 1 and exactly 0 at every lag beyond that -- there is no direct dependence on X_(t-2), X_(t-3), etc. once X_(t-1) is accounted for, since the model's entire generating equation only ever references one lag back. The lag-1 value near 0.8 recovers the true phi used to simulate the data; the near-zero values at lags 2-4 (small nonzero numbers due to finite-sample noise, not a real effect) reflect that any apparent correlation at those lags in the raw ACF was fully transmitted through lag 1 and had nothing left over once that lag was controlled for in the underlying regression PACF computes.

exercises.solutionExplanation: The theoretical signatures are: a pure AR(p) process has a PACF that cuts off after lag p (and an ACF that decays gradually, with no clean cutoff at all), while a pure MA(q) process has the reverse -- an ACF that cuts off after lag q and a PACF that decays gradually. The original code reads the AR order from the ACF's cutoff and the MA order from the PACF's cutoff, exactly backwards from the correct convention. On this genuinely AR(1) series, the ACF decays smoothly and may never cleanly cross the 0.1 threshold within 8 lags (or crosses it much later than lag 1, giving a misleadingly large p_candidate), while the PACF correctly cuts off right after lag 1. Swapping which array feeds which candidate fixes the logic and correctly recovers p=1 as the AR order, with q read from wherever the ACF actually settles near zero.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly defines the partial autocorrelation function (PACF) at lag k, and distinguishes it from the ACF at lag k?

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague what distinguishes the ACF from the PACF conceptually, why a pure AR(p) process and a pure MA(q) process show opposite cutoff-versus-decay signatures in the two functions, and why a practitioner shouldn't stop at reading the plots alone when choosing an ARIMA order.
assessments.modelAnswer: The ACF at lag k is just the raw correlation between a series and a copy of itself shifted back k steps -- it doesn't care whether that correlation is direct or is really being transmitted indirectly through shorter lags sitting in between. The PACF at lag k asks a more specific question: once you've already accounted for the linear effect of every shorter lag (1 through k-1), how much additional correlation is left at exactly lag k? That extra conditioning is what lets PACF isolate a lag's own, direct contribution rather than mixing it with everything transmitted through nearer lags. This distinction is exactly why a pure AR(p) process and a pure MA(q) process show opposite signatures: an AR(p) process's entire dependence on the past runs through its p most recent lags, so once you control for those p lags in a regression, no longer lag adds anything further -- the PACF cuts off sharply right after lag p, even though the ACF keeps showing decaying-but-nonzero correlation at every lag because those longer-lag relationships really are present, just transmitted rather than direct. An MA(q) process is the mirror image: its observed values share no common shock terms once you're more than q steps apart, so its ACF cuts off cleanly after lag q, but expressing that same structure as a regression on past observed values takes an ever-growing autoregression to approximate, which is why its PACF decays gradually instead of cutting off. In practice, though, real series are rarely purely one or the other, and the sample versions of these functions are noisy estimates with confidence bands, so a practitioner uses the plots only to shortlist a couple of plausible (p, q) candidates, then actually fits those candidates and compares them with a penalized criterion like AIC or BIC, and checks the winning model's residuals for any leftover autocorrelation, before trusting a final chosen order.

concepts.title: Unit Root Tests: Augmented Dickey-Fuller and KPSS
concepts.description: A unit root in a series' characteristic equation is the formal condition that produces non-stationarity, and the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test (null: a unit root is present) and the KPSS test (null: the series is stationary -- the opposite convention) are the two standard, and deliberately complementary, hypothesis tests practitioners run together to formally decide whether a series needs differencing before modeling.
learningObjectives: Explain what a unit root is in the characteristic equation of an autoregressive process and why its presence implies non-stationarity.
State the null and alternative hypotheses of the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test and interpret its p-value correctly.
State the null and alternative hypotheses of the KPSS test and explain how they are the logical opposite of the ADF test's hypotheses.
Run both ADF and KPSS on a series using statsmodels and reconcile agreeing or conflicting results using the standard four-way decision table.
Explain how the outcome of a unit root test formally answers the practical question of whether, and how much, to difference a series before modeling it.

sections.heading: What a Unit Root Is, and Why It Means Non-Stationarity
sections.body:
Go back to the AR(1) equation from earlier in this module, `X_t = phi * X_(t-1) + eps_t`, and rewrite it in terms of its **characteristic equation**: `1 - phi*z = 0`, which has a single root at `z = 1/phi`. The stability condition `|phi| < 1` from the AR/MA/ARIMA concept is exactly equivalent to saying this root lies strictly outside the unit circle (`|z| > 1`). A **unit root** is the boundary case: a root sitting exactly *on* the unit circle, `|z| = 1`, which for AR(1) means `phi = 1` exactly -- and `phi = 1` turns the equation into `X_t = X_(t-1) + eps_t`, precisely the random walk used as the non-stationary example throughout this module.

It's worth being explicit about *why* a unit root breaks stationarity, rather than just accepting it as a definition. With `phi = 1`, recursively substituting gives `X_t = X_0 + eps_1 + eps_2 + ... + eps_t` -- every single shock the process has ever experienced is carried forward with a permanent weight of exactly 1, never decaying. Its variance is `Var(X_t) = t * sigma^2`, which grows without bound as `t` increases rather than settling at a fixed constant, directly violating weak stationarity's constant-variance requirement (from the very first concept in this module). Contrast this with `|phi| < 1`, where each shock's weight decays geometrically and the process's variance converges to a fixed constant, `sigma^2 / (1 - phi^2)`, as `t` grows. For a general AR(p) process, the same idea generalizes: stationarity requires every root of the characteristic polynomial `1 - phi_1*z - phi_2*z^2 - ... - phi_p*z^p = 0` to lie strictly outside the unit circle; any root landing exactly on it means the process is **integrated** (non-stationary, but stationary after differencing) -- which is exactly what the "I" in ARIMA is there to fix, tying this concept directly back to how `d` gets chosen.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 500
eps = rng.normal(size=n)

random_walk = np.cumsum(eps)                        # phi = 1 exactly -- a unit root

stationary_ar1 = np.zeros(n)                          # phi = 0.8 -- no unit root
for t in range(1, n):
    stationary_ar1[t] = 0.8 * stationary_ar1[t - 1] + eps[t]

print("random walk variance, first half vs second half:",
      round(random_walk[:250].var(), 1), "vs", round(random_walk[250:].var(), 1))
print("stationary AR(1) variance, first half vs second half:",
      round(stationary_ar1[:250].var(), 1), "vs", round(stationary_ar1[250:].var(), 1))
```

The random walk's second-half variance should come out roughly double its first-half variance -- direct numeric confirmation of `Var(X_t)` growing linearly with `t` -- while the stationary AR(1) process's two halves should land close to each other, both hovering near the theoretical `sigma^2 / (1 - 0.8^2)`. This variance-growth pattern is the concrete, checkable fingerprint a unit root leaves behind, and it's exactly what the formal tests in the rest of this concept are built to detect statistically, rather than by eyeballing a variance split like this.

sections.heading: The Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test: Null = Non-Stationary
sections.body:
The **Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test** formalizes the unit-root check into a hypothesis test. Its null and alternative hypotheses are: **H0: the series has a unit root (it is non-stationary)**; **H1: the series is stationary** (or stationary around a deterministic trend, depending on the test's exact specification). Mechanically, ADF regresses the first difference `delta X_t = X_t - X_(t-1)` on `X_(t-1)`, a constant (and optionally a trend term), and enough lagged difference terms `delta X_(t-1), delta X_(t-2), ...` to soak up any leftover autocorrelation in the residuals -- that augmentation with extra lagged difference terms is exactly what the "Augmented" in the test's name refers to, distinguishing it from the simpler, un-augmented Dickey-Fuller test it generalizes. The test statistic is the t-statistic on the `X_(t-1)` coefficient, but critically, it does **not** follow a standard t-distribution -- it follows a special, non-standard distribution derived by Dickey and Fuller specifically for this test, which is why you read off a p-value from the test's own tables (or, in practice, however statsmodels reports it) rather than a generic t-table.

The **interpretation rule** that matters in practice: a **small p-value** (conventionally below 0.05) lets you **reject H0**, giving evidence that the series **is stationary**. A **large p-value** means you **fail to reject H0**, i.e. you don't have sufficient evidence to rule out a unit root, so you'd typically proceed as if the series is non-stationary (with an important caveat about what "fail to reject" does and doesn't prove, addressed directly in this concept's misconceptions).

```python
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 500
eps = rng.normal(size=n)

random_walk = np.cumsum(eps)
stationary_ar1 = np.zeros(n)
for t in range(1, n):
    stationary_ar1[t] = 0.8 * stationary_ar1[t - 1] + eps[t]

rw_stat, rw_pvalue, *_ = adfuller(random_walk)
ar_stat, ar_pvalue, *_ = adfuller(stationary_ar1)

print(f"random walk:       ADF stat={rw_stat:.3f}, p-value={rw_pvalue:.3f}")
print(f"stationary AR(1):  ADF stat={ar_stat:.3f}, p-value={ar_pvalue:.3f}")
```

The random walk's p-value should come back large (typically well above 0.05), meaning ADF fails to reject the unit-root null, correctly flagging the series as (consistent with) non-stationary. The stationary AR(1) series' p-value should come back small (typically well below 0.05), meaning ADF rejects the unit-root null and correctly provides evidence of stationarity -- exactly matching what was already known by construction in each case, which is the point of running the test on data with a known ground truth before trusting it on data where you don't know the answer in advance.

sections.heading: The KPSS Test: Null = Stationary (The Opposite Convention)
sections.body:
The **KPSS test** (Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin) is built around **exactly the opposite null hypothesis** from ADF: **H0: the series is (trend-)stationary**; **H1: the series has a unit root**. Mechanically, KPSS works quite differently from ADF -- it regresses the series on a constant (and optionally a deterministic trend), accumulates the partial sums of the residuals from that regression, and builds a Lagrange-multiplier-type statistic from how much those partial sums drift, which grows large specifically when the residuals fail to behave like stationary noise around the fitted level or trend.

The **interpretation rule for KPSS is the mirror image of ADF's**, precisely because the null hypothesis itself is reversed: a **small p-value** (below 0.05) lets you **reject H0**, giving evidence the series **has a unit root (is non-stationary)**. A **large p-value** means you **fail to reject H0**, consistent with the series being stationary. This reversal is, without exaggeration, the single most common practical point of confusion in applied unit-root testing: a low p-value means "stationary" under ADF but means "non-stationary" under KPSS, and reading one test's p-value using the other's interpretation rule produces a conclusion that is not just imprecise but flatly backwards.

```python
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import kpss

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 500
eps = rng.normal(size=n)

random_walk = np.cumsum(eps)
stationary_ar1 = np.zeros(n)
for t in range(1, n):
    stationary_ar1[t] = 0.8 * stationary_ar1[t - 1] + eps[t]

rw_stat, rw_pvalue, *_ = kpss(random_walk, regression="c")
ar_stat, ar_pvalue, *_ = kpss(stationary_ar1, regression="c")

print(f"random walk:       KPSS stat={rw_stat:.3f}, p-value={rw_pvalue:.3f}")
print(f"stationary AR(1):  KPSS stat={ar_stat:.3f}, p-value={ar_pvalue:.3f}")
```

The random walk's KPSS p-value should come back small, letting you reject KPSS's stationarity null and correctly conclude non-stationarity. The stationary AR(1) series' KPSS p-value should come back large, meaning you fail to reject the stationarity null, again correctly matching the known ground truth. Note the *direction* of each conclusion relative to the p-value is opposite to what ADF produced on the same two series in the previous section, even though both tests reach the same correct real-world conclusion about each series -- which is exactly the reversed-null relationship this section exists to make unmistakable.

sections.heading: Running Both Together: The Decision Table Practitioners Actually Use
sections.body:
Because ADF and KPSS have opposite null hypotheses and different statistical power characteristics (each is better at detecting certain kinds of departures from its own null than the other), practitioners routinely run **both** and reconcile the results using a standard four-way decision table, built from what each test concludes:

- **ADF rejects H0 (says stationary) AND KPSS fails to reject H0 (says stationary):** both tests agree -- treat the series as stationary with reasonably high confidence.
- **ADF fails to reject H0 (says non-stationary) AND KPSS rejects H0 (says non-stationary):** both tests agree -- treat the series as non-stationary, and difference it (increase `d`) before modeling.
- **ADF rejects H0 (says stationary) AND KPSS rejects H0 (says non-stationary):** the tests conflict. This specific combination often signals a **trend-stationary** series -- one that is stationary once a deterministic trend is removed, but whose raw (undetrended) form still shows the trend-driven non-stationarity KPSS is picking up. The practical fix here is usually detrending rather than differencing.
- **ADF fails to reject H0 (says non-stationary) AND KPSS fails to reject H0 (says stationary):** the tests conflict in the other direction -- generally read as inconclusive, often the result of low test power on a short or noisy sample. Widening the sample, inspecting the series visually, or leaning on residual diagnostics after a tentative model fit becomes the practical tiebreaker.

This decision table is, quite literally, the formal statistical answer to the everyday practitioner question this module keeps returning to: **should I difference this series before modeling it?** Rather than eyeballing a plot and guessing, running ADF and KPSS together gives that judgment call a known, quantified error rate, and the outcome directly determines the differencing order `d` fed into ARIMA(p, d, q) from earlier in this module.

```python
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller, kpss

def recommend_differencing(series, alpha=0.05):
    adf_pvalue = adfuller(series)[1]
    kpss_pvalue = kpss(series, regression="c")[1]

    adf_says_stationary = adf_pvalue < alpha
    kpss_says_stationary = kpss_pvalue >= alpha

    if adf_says_stationary and kpss_says_stationary:
        return "stationary -- no differencing needed", adf_pvalue, kpss_pvalue
    if not adf_says_stationary and not kpss_says_stationary:
        return "non-stationary -- difference the series (increase d)", adf_pvalue, kpss_pvalue
    if adf_says_stationary and not kpss_says_stationary:
        return "conflicting -- likely trend-stationary, consider detrending instead of differencing", adf_pvalue, kpss_pvalue
    return "conflicting -- inconclusive, likely low test power; inspect visually or gather more data", adf_pvalue, kpss_pvalue

# recommend_differencing(some_series) -> a plain-language recommendation plus both p-values
```

This function is a direct, executable encoding of the four-way table above -- and it's worth noticing that it never claims certainty in the two "agree" cases either, only "reasonably high confidence" or a directional recommendation, because both tests remain probabilistic tools with known false-positive and false-negative rates, not oracles. The next concept in this module (Markov Chains and Hidden Markov Models) shifts to a different but related kind of stochastic process; this differencing decision is the last piece of the classical stationarity-to-ARIMA-order pipeline this module has been building since its very first concept.

examples.title: ADF on a Random Walk vs. a Stationary AR(1) Series
examples.code:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

rng = np.random.default_rng(20)
n = 400
eps = rng.normal(size=n)

random_walk = np.cumsum(eps)
stationary_ar1 = np.zeros(n)
for t in range(1, n):
    stationary_ar1[t] = 0.75 * stationary_ar1[t - 1] + eps[t]

for name, series in [("random walk", random_walk), ("stationary AR(1)", stationary_ar1)]:
    stat, pvalue, *_ = adfuller(series)
    verdict = "reject H0 -> evidence of stationarity" if pvalue < 0.05 else "fail to reject H0 -> consistent with a unit root"
    print(f"{name}: ADF stat={stat:.3f}, p={pvalue:.4f} -> {verdict}")
examples.explanation: The random walk should report a large p-value, leading to 'fail to reject H0', which under ADF's null of 'has a unit root' means the test correctly cannot rule out non-stationarity. The stationary AR(1) series should report a small p-value, leading to 'reject H0', correctly providing evidence of stationarity. Both outcomes match what's already known about each series by construction, which is exactly why testing on synthetic data with a known ground truth first is good practice before trusting the test on a real series where the true answer is unknown.

    print(f"{name}: KPSS stat={stat:.3f}, p={pvalue:.4f} -> {verdict}")
examples.explanation: The random walk should report a small KPSS p-value, leading to 'reject H0', which under KPSS's null of 'is stationary' correctly means evidence of a unit root. The stationary AR(1) series should report a large KPSS p-value, leading to 'fail to reject H0', correctly consistent with stationarity. Note that a small p-value meant 'evidence of stationarity' under ADF in the previous example but means 'evidence against stationarity' here -- the exact same-looking number requires an opposite reading depending on which test produced it, which is the whole reason this concept insists on stating each test's null hypothesis explicitly every time rather than relying on p-value size alone.

examples.title: A Combined ADF + KPSS Differencing Recommendation Function
examples.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller, kpss

def recommend_differencing(series, alpha=0.05):
    adf_p = adfuller(series)[1]
    kpss_p = kpss(series, regression="c")[1]
    adf_stationary = adf_p < alpha
    kpss_stationary = kpss_p >= alpha

    if adf_stationary and kpss_stationary:
        verdict = "stationary -- no differencing needed"
    elif not adf_stationary and not kpss_stationary:
        verdict = "non-stationary -- difference the series"
    elif adf_stationary and not kpss_stationary:
        verdict = "conflicting -- likely trend-stationary, consider detrending"
    else:
        verdict = "conflicting -- inconclusive, likely low power"
    return verdict, adf_p, kpss_p

rng = np.random.default_rng(30)
t = np.arange(300)
trend_stationary = 0.05 * t + rng.normal(scale=1.0, size=300)   # stationary AROUND a trend

print(recommend_differencing(trend_stationary))
examples.explanation: A trend-stationary series like this one -- noise fluctuating around a fixed deterministic trend line, rather than a trend produced by an accumulating random walk -- is exactly the case the decision table flags as 'conflicting': ADF's regression includes a way to account for the deterministic trend and can reject its unit-root null, while a basic KPSS test run with regression='c' (constant only, no trend term) may still reject its stationarity null because the raw series' level clearly isn't constant. This is precisely the four-way table's 'ADF says stationary, KPSS says non-stationary' cell, and the practical fix -- detrending rather than differencing -- avoids the over-differencing problem introduced back in the AR/MA/ARIMA concept.

misconceptions.description: ADF and KPSS test the same null hypothesis, so a low p-value means the same thing for both, and you only really need to run one of them.
misconceptions.clarification: The two tests have exactly opposite null hypotheses: ADF's null is 'a unit root is present (non-stationary)', so a low p-value there means rejecting non-stationarity, i.e. evidence of stationarity. KPSS's null is 'the series is stationary', so a low p-value there means rejecting stationarity, i.e. evidence of a unit root -- the opposite conclusion from the same-looking low p-value. Practitioners run both precisely because they can disagree, and that disagreement itself is diagnostic (for instance, flagging a trend-stationary series), which running only one of the two tests would never reveal.

misconceptions.description: A large ADF p-value (failing to reject the unit-root null) definitively proves the series is non-stationary.
misconceptions.clarification: Failing to reject a null hypothesis is never the same as proving it true -- it only means the data didn't provide strong enough evidence to rule it out, which can happen either because the series really is non-stationary, or simply because the test has low statistical power on that particular sample (short series, structural breaks, or a phi very close to but technically inside the stability boundary are all classic causes of low power). Treating 'fail to reject' as certainty is the same general statistical error as treating any other hypothesis test's null-hypothesis retention as proof, and it's exactly why practitioners cross-check with KPSS, inspect the series visually, and consider sample size and structural stability rather than trusting a single test's p-value as a final verdict.

A small p-value under ADF means you reject the unit-root null -- that's evidence FOR stationarity, i.e. differencing is probably NOT needed, which is the opposite of what the buggy function returns.
Flip the condition: 'needs differencing' should correspond to a LARGE p-value (failing to reject the unit-root null), not a small one.

import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

def needs_differencing(series, alpha=0.05):
    stat, pvalue, *_ = adfuller(series)
    # FIXED: a small p-value rejects the unit-root null -> evidence of stationarity -> no differencing needed
    if pvalue < alpha:
        return False   # evidence of stationarity
    return True   # failed to reject unit-root null -> treat as needing differencing

rng = np.random.default_rng(60)
stationary_series = np.zeros(400)
eps = rng.normal(size=400)
for t in range(1, 400):
    stationary_series[t] = 0.6 * stationary_series[t - 1] + eps[t]

exercises.solutionExplanation: ADF's null hypothesis is 'the series has a unit root (is non-stationary)', so a small p-value means REJECTING that null, which is evidence the series IS stationary -- exactly the opposite of what the buggy code concluded by returning True ('needs differencing') on a small p-value. The fix flips the boolean logic: a small p-value (reject H0) means stationary, so differencing is not needed; a large p-value (fail to reject H0) means the unit root can't be ruled out, so differencing is the safer default. Getting this backwards is a genuinely common bug precisely because 'small p-value = something significant is happening' is true in general, but which specific conclusion that significance supports depends entirely on which hypothesis is the null -- exactly the confusion this concept's misconceptions call out directly.

This particular conflict pattern is the standard signature of a trend-stationary series, where the practical remedy is usually detrending rather than blind differencing. Option A and B both incorrectly describe this as agreement, when it's actually the conflicting cell of the four-way decision table. assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague why ADF and KPSS have opposite null hypotheses, how to correctly read a p-value from each, and why running both together -- and reconciling any disagreement -- is the standard formal way to decide whether a series needs differencing before modeling.
assessments.modelAnswer: A unit root exists when a root of a series' characteristic equation lands exactly on the boundary of the AR stability condition, and its presence is what makes a process non-stationary -- shocks never decay, and variance grows without bound over time rather than settling at a fixed value. ADF and KPSS are the two standard hypothesis tests for detecting this, but they are built around deliberately opposite null hypotheses: ADF's null is that a unit root is present (the series is non-stationary), so a small p-value lets you reject that null and concludes the series is likely stationary, while a large p-value means you cannot rule out a unit root. KPSS flips this around entirely -- its null is that the series is stationary, so a small p-value there lets you reject stationarity and concludes the series likely has a unit root, while a large p-value is consistent with stationarity. The exact same-looking small p-value therefore means opposite things depending on which test produced it, which is the single most common point of confusion in applying these tests, and getting it backwards produces a conclusion that is not just imprecise but flipped. Because the two tests have different statistical power against different kinds of departures from stationarity, and because their nulls are logical opposites, practitioners run both together and reconcile the results with a four-way table: both tests agreeing the series is stationary or both agreeing it's non-stationary gives real confidence in that direction; ADF saying stationary while KPSS says non-stationary often flags a trend-stationary series calling for detrending rather than differencing; and the reverse disagreement is usually inconclusive, often due to low test power on a short or noisy sample. This combined procedure is exactly the formal, quantifiable version of the everyday practitioner question 'should I difference this series before modeling it,' replacing a visual guess with a decision backed by two independent, known-error-rate statistical tests, and it directly sets the differencing order d that feeds into an ARIMA(p, d, q) model.

concepts.title: Markov Chains and Hidden Markov Models
concepts.description: The Markov property says a chain's future depends on its full history only through its current state, transition matrices and their powers give one-step and multi-step transition probabilities, stationary distributions describe where the chain settles in the long run, and Hidden Markov Models add a layer of unobserved states -- the direct conceptual ancestor of modern sequence models and still used today for tasks like part-of-speech tagging.
learningObjectives: State the Markov property precisely and explain why it makes a chain's future depend only on its current state, not its full history, without implying the process has no memory at all.
Construct and use a transition probability matrix, and compute multi-step transition probabilities via matrix powers.
Define a stationary distribution of a Markov chain, compute it for a small example, and connect the concept to weak stationarity for time series.
Explain how a Hidden Markov Model extends a Markov chain by adding a hidden state layer that emits observable outputs, distinguishing transition probabilities from emission probabilities.
Describe a concrete HMM application such as part-of-speech tagging, and explain why Markov chains and HMMs are considered a conceptual ancestor of modern sequence models.

sections.heading: The Markov Property: Memorylessness in a Precise Sense
sections.body:
A discrete-time, discrete-state **Markov chain** is a sequence of random variables `X_0, X_1, X_2, ...`, each taking a value from a fixed set of states, that satisfies the **Markov property**: `P(X_(t+1) = j | X_t = i, X_(t-1), X_(t-2), ..., X_0) = P(X_(t+1) = j | X_t = i)`. In plain language, once you know the current state, knowing the *entire* history that led up to it adds nothing further to your ability to predict what happens next -- the future is conditionally independent of the past, given the present.

This is easy to over-interpret as "the process has no memory at all," which is a genuine and important misreading to correct up front. The Markov property is about the *transition rule*, not about how much real-world history the current state is allowed to summarize -- a state can, by design, be engineered to encode as much of the relevant past as you need. A chain whose state is literally "the last 3 words typed" still satisfies the Markov property with respect to *that* state definition, even though it clearly depends on more than just the immediately preceding instant; what's memoryless is that, given this specific state, nothing about *how* the process arrived there changes the transition probabilities. Choosing what the state represents is a real design decision with real consequences, not a limitation baked into the mathematics itself.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
states = ["Sunny", "Rainy"]
transition = {
    "Sunny": {"Sunny": 0.8, "Rainy": 0.2},
    "Rainy": {"Sunny": 0.4, "Rainy": 0.6},
}

def step(current_state):
    options = list(transition[current_state].keys())
    probs = list(transition[current_state].values())
    return rng.choice(options, p=probs)

# Simulate two independent 5-day paths that both happen to pass through "Sunny" on day 2 --
# the Markov property says day-3-onward behavior should not depend on how day 2's "Sunny" was reached.
path_a = ["Sunny", "Rainy", "Sunny"]
path_b = ["Rainy", "Rainy", "Sunny"]
print("Both paths reach 'Sunny' at day 2 via different histories.")
print("day-3 transition probabilities depend ONLY on 'Sunny':", transition["Sunny"])
```

Regardless of which specific history (`path_a` or `path_b`) led to landing on "Sunny" at day 2, the code has no mechanism to even look at that history when deciding day 3's probabilities -- `transition["Sunny"]` is looked up by the current state alone. That's the Markov property made completely concrete: the dictionary literally cannot see anything but the current key.

sections.heading: Transition Matrices and Multi-Step Transitions
sections.body:
A Markov chain's **transition matrix** `P` collects every one-step transition probability into a single object: `P[i, j] = P(X_(t+1) = j | X_t = i)`. Every row of `P` is a full probability distribution over "where do I go next, given I'm currently in state i," so every row must sum to exactly 1 (a state has to go *somewhere*, including possibly staying put).

Multi-step transition probabilities follow directly from matrix multiplication, via a result called the **Chapman-Kolmogorov equation**: the probability of going from state `i` to state `j` in exactly 2 steps is `P(X_(t+2)=j | X_t=i) = sum over k of P[i,k] * P[k,j]`, summing over every possible intermediate state `k` the chain could have passed through -- which is exactly the definition of matrix multiplication, `(P @ P)[i, j]`. This generalizes cleanly: the `n`-step transition probabilities are given by the `n`-th matrix power, `P^n`.

```python
import numpy as np

states = ["Sunny", "Rainy"]
P = np.array([
    [0.8, 0.2],   # from Sunny: 80% Sunny, 20% Rainy
    [0.4, 0.6],   # from Rainy: 40% Sunny, 60% Rainy
])

print("rows sum to 1:", P.sum(axis=1))

P2 = P @ P                          # 2-step transition probabilities
P5 = np.linalg.matrix_power(P, 5)   # 5-step transition probabilities
P50 = np.linalg.matrix_power(P, 50)  # 50-step transition probabilities

print("P^2:\n", np.round(P2, 3))
print("P^5:\n", np.round(P5, 3))
print("P^50:\n", np.round(P50, 3))
```

Watch what happens as the power grows: `P^50`'s two rows should end up nearly identical to each other, both converging to essentially the same pair of numbers -- meaning that after enough steps, the probability of being in "Sunny" 50 days out is *almost the same number* whether you started Sunny or Rainy today. The chain has "forgotten" its starting point entirely; it's converged to a single long-run distribution over states, which is exactly the stationary distribution introduced in the next section.

sections.heading: Stationary Distributions: Where the Chain Settles
sections.body:
A **stationary distribution** of a Markov chain is a row vector `pi` (a probability distribution over the states, so its entries are non-negative and sum to 1) satisfying `pi @ P = pi` -- if the chain's current state distribution is `pi`, then applying one more transition step leaves the distribution unchanged. Under mild conditions (the chain needs to be **irreducible** -- every state reachable from every other state -- and **aperiodic** -- it doesn't cycle through states in a rigid, fixed-length loop), this `pi` is unique, and the chain's distribution converges to it from *any* starting distribution as the number of steps grows, exactly the convergence already observed numerically with `P^50` in the previous section.

This naming is not a coincidence relative to the very first concept in this module: a stationary distribution here is the discrete-Markov-chain analogue of weak stationarity for a continuous-valued time series -- in both cases, "stationary" means a state (a full probability distribution here, a set of moments there) that dynamics leave unchanged going forward.

```python
import numpy as np

P = np.array([
    [0.8, 0.2],
    [0.4, 0.6],
])

# Solve pi @ P = pi, sum(pi) = 1 via the eigenvector of P^T with eigenvalue 1.
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(P.T)
stationary_index = np.argmin(np.abs(eigenvalues - 1.0))
pi = np.real(eigenvectors[:, stationary_index])
pi = pi / pi.sum()

print("stationary distribution pi:", np.round(pi, 3))
print("check pi @ P == pi:", np.round(pi @ P, 3))

P50 = np.linalg.matrix_power(P, 50)
print("P^50 rows (should both match pi):\n", np.round(P50, 3))
```

`pi` should come out close to `[0.667, 0.333]` -- roughly two-thirds Sunny, one-third Rainy in the long run -- and both rows of `P^50` should closely match this same vector, confirming numerically that the eigenvector solution and the brute-force matrix-power convergence agree. This gives you two independent, cross-checkable ways to compute the same long-run answer, which is a good habit whenever a closed-form solution and a simulation both apply to the same problem.

sections.heading: Hidden Markov Models: Adding a Layer You Can't Observe
sections.body:
A **Hidden Markov Model (HMM)** adds one more layer on top of an ordinary Markov chain: the chain's states, `Z_t`, are never directly observed -- they're **hidden** -- and at each step, the current hidden state emits an observable output `X_t` according to an **emission distribution** (often written as an emission matrix `B`, where `B[i, k] = P(X_t = k | Z_t = i)`), which is a genuinely different object from the transition matrix `A` governing how the hidden states themselves evolve. You only ever get to see the sequence of emitted outputs `X_1, X_2, ..., X_T`; the goal is almost always to infer something about the hidden sequence `Z_1, ..., Z_T` that plausibly produced it.

A concrete toy example makes the moving parts tangible: imagine hidden weather states {Rainy, Sunny} with some transition matrix `A` governing how the weather itself evolves day to day, and an emission matrix `B` describing the probability of observing someone doing {Walk, Shop, Clean} conditioned on the day's (hidden, unobserved-by-you) weather. Given only a sequence of observed activities, an HMM lets you compute both the overall likelihood of that observed sequence, and, at each time step, a probability distribution over what the hidden weather most likely was -- without ever directly seeing the weather itself.

```python
import numpy as np

states = ["Rainy", "Sunny"]
observations = ["Walk", "Shop", "Clean"]

A = np.array([        # hidden-state transition matrix
    [0.7, 0.3],        # from Rainy: 70% Rainy, 30% Sunny
    [0.4, 0.6],        # from Sunny: 40% Rainy, 60% Sunny
])
B = np.array([        # emission matrix: P(observation | hidden state)
    [0.1, 0.4, 0.5],   # Rainy  -> P(Walk), P(Shop), P(Clean)
    [0.6, 0.3, 0.1],   # Sunny  -> P(Walk), P(Shop), P(Clean)
])
pi0 = np.array([0.6, 0.4])   # initial distribution over hidden states

obs_sequence = [0, 2, 1]   # Walk, Clean, Shop  (indices into `observations`)

def forward_algorithm(obs_sequence, A, B, pi0):
    n_states = A.shape[0]
    T = len(obs_sequence)
    alpha = np.zeros((T, n_states))
    alpha[0] = pi0 * B[:, obs_sequence[0]]
    for t in range(1, T):
        for j in range(n_states):
            alpha[t, j] = np.sum(alpha[t - 1] * A[:, j]) * B[j, obs_sequence[t]]
    likelihood = alpha[-1].sum()
    filtered = alpha / alpha.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)   # normalize each row to get P(hidden state | obs so far)
    return likelihood, filtered

likelihood, filtered_probs = forward_algorithm(obs_sequence, A, B, pi0)
print("P(observed sequence 'Walk, Clean, Shop'):", round(likelihood, 5))
print("filtered hidden-state probabilities per day:\n", np.round(filtered_probs, 3))
```

`forward_algorithm` is a compact, from-scratch implementation of the dynamic-programming **forward algorithm**: `alpha[t, j]` accumulates the probability of having observed everything up to time `t` *and* being in hidden state `j` at time `t`, built up recursively from `alpha[t-1]` via the same transition-matrix-multiplication idea from the earlier sections of this concept, then weighted by how likely state `j` is to have produced the actual observation seen at time `t`. The full **Viterbi algorithm** (not implemented here, but a close cousin of this one) instead finds the single *most likely* hidden state sequence, rather than the marginal probability at each step separately, using a nearly identical recursion with `max` in place of `sum`.

HMMs were the dominant technique for **part-of-speech tagging** (hidden state = grammatical tag, observed output = the actual word) and speech recognition (hidden state = phoneme, observed output = an acoustic frame) for years before neural sequence models displaced them for large-scale production use. Their core design pattern -- a compact hidden state, updated one step at a time as new input arrives, that summarizes everything relevant about the sequence so far -- is exactly the pattern later generalized by an RNN's hidden state (dropping the discrete-state and strict-Markov restrictions) and, later still, by attention-based sequence models. Plain Markov chains and small HMMs are still used directly today for lightweight sequence tasks -- simple text generators, baseline POS taggers, bioinformatics sequence models -- precisely where a full neural sequence model would be needless overkill, and working through them by hand, as this concept has, is the cleanest available path to real intuition before tackling a full neural sequence-modeling course.

examples.explanation: Every row of P sums to exactly 1.0, confirming it's a legitimate transition matrix -- each row genuinely is a probability distribution over 'where next.' P^2 gives two-step transition probabilities, already noticeably different from the raw one-step matrix as multiple paths get mixed together. P^20's three rows should be nearly identical to each other, meaning the chain has converged to essentially the same long-run distribution over Sunny/Cloudy/Rainy regardless of which state it started in -- the numeric signature of having reached the stationary distribution.

examples.title: Simulating a Random Trajectory Through the Chain
examples.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
states = ["Sunny", "Cloudy", "Rainy"]
P = np.array([
    [0.6, 0.3, 0.1],
    [0.3, 0.4, 0.3],
    [0.2, 0.3, 0.5],
])

def simulate_chain(P, states, start_index, n_steps):
    current = start_index
    path = [states[current]]
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        current = rng.choice(len(states), p=P[current])
        path.append(states[current])
    return path

trajectory = simulate_chain(P, states, start_index=0, n_steps=15)
print(" -> ".join(trajectory))

# Empirically estimate the long-run fraction of time spent in each state from one long run.
long_run = simulate_chain(P, states, start_index=0, n_steps=20000)
from collections import Counter
counts = Counter(long_run)
total = len(long_run)
print({state: round(counts[state] / total, 3) for state in states})
examples.explanation: The 15-step trajectory shows one concrete, plausible path through the chain, sampled at each step directly from the current state's row of P using np.random.choice, which is the direct simulation-based analogue of the abstract 'multiply by P' operation. The 20,000-step empirical fraction of time spent in each state should closely match the stationary distribution pi computed analytically elsewhere in this concept (via the eigenvector method) -- a long enough single trajectory's time-average converges to the same distribution the ensemble-average matrix-power calculation converges to, a basic instance of the ergodic property irreducible, aperiodic chains have.

examples.title: Toy HMM: Inferring Likely Hidden Weather From Observed Activities
examples.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[0.7, 0.3], [0.4, 0.6]])       # hidden transition: Rainy, Sunny
B = np.array([[0.1, 0.4, 0.5], [0.6, 0.3, 0.1]])  # emission: Walk, Shop, Clean
pi0 = np.array([0.6, 0.4])

def forward_algorithm(obs_sequence, A, B, pi0):
    T, n_states = len(obs_sequence), A.shape[0]
    alpha = np.zeros((T, n_states))
    alpha[0] = pi0 * B[:, obs_sequence[0]]
    for t in range(1, T):
        for j in range(n_states):
            alpha[t, j] = np.sum(alpha[t - 1] * A[:, j]) * B[j, obs_sequence[t]]
    return alpha

obs_walk_walk_clean = [0, 0, 2]   # Walk, Walk, Clean
obs_clean_clean_clean = [2, 2, 2]  # Clean, Clean, Clean

for name, obs in [("Walk,Walk,Clean", obs_walk_walk_clean), ("Clean,Clean,Clean", obs_clean_clean_clean)]:
    alpha = forward_algorithm(obs, A, B, pi0)
    filtered = alpha / alpha.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    print(f"{name}: P(sequence)={alpha[-1].sum():.5f}, final day P(Rainy)={filtered[-1, 0]:.3f}")
examples.explanation: Two consecutive Walk observations followed by Clean should push the filtered probability toward Sunny on the final day (Walk is far more likely to be emitted by Sunny than Rainy, 0.6 vs 0.1), while three consecutive Clean observations should push the final-day probability strongly toward Rainy (Clean is emitted with probability 0.5 under Rainy versus only 0.1 under Sunny). Note the model never observes the weather directly in either case -- every conclusion about the hidden state comes entirely from how consistent each possible hidden-state sequence is with the emission probabilities of what was actually observed, which is the entire inferential point of an HMM.

misconceptions.description: The Markov property means the process has no memory at all -- it can't meaningfully use any information from before the current instant.
misconceptions.clarification: The Markov property only says the future is conditionally independent of the past GIVEN the current state -- it says nothing about how much real-world history that current state is allowed to summarize. A state can be engineered to encode an arbitrary amount of relevant history (for instance, defining the state as 'the last k observations' rather than just the single most recent one), and the chain built on that richer state definition still satisfies the Markov property with respect to it. 'Memoryless' describes the transition rule's dependence structure, not an absolute limit on how much of the past matters to the process as a whole.

misconceptions.description: In a Hidden Markov Model, the observed outputs are effectively the same thing as the hidden states -- 'hidden' just means the states haven't been looked at yet, and can be read straight off the observations.
misconceptions.clarification: Hidden states in an HMM are never directly observable even in principle from the emitted outputs alone -- the entire premise of the model is that a single observation could plausibly have been emitted by several different hidden states, each with some nonzero probability under the emission distribution. Recovering information about the hidden state sequence requires genuine probabilistic inference over both the transition and emission probabilities (the forward algorithm for marginal probabilities, the Viterbi algorithm for the single most likely sequence) -- it is not something you can simply read off the observed data directly, no matter how the observations happen to look.

exercises.prompt: Given this transition matrix and initial state distribution, what does the code print for the state distribution after 2 steps, and how is it computed?
exercises.code:
import numpy as np

P = np.array([
    [0.9, 0.1],
    [0.5, 0.5],
])
pi0 = np.array([1.0, 0.0])   # start with certainty in state 0

pi1 = pi0 @ P
pi2 = pi1 @ P
print(np.round(pi2, 3))
hints: pi0 @ P gives the state distribution after 1 step -- compute that first by hand: it's just pi0's weighted combination of P's rows.
Since pi0 = [1.0, 0.0], pi0 @ P should simply equal the first row of P.
Apply the same 'multiply by P' operation one more time to pi1 to get pi2 -- equivalent to computing pi0 @ (P @ P), i.e. the 2-step transition probabilities starting from state 0.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Starting with certainty in state 0 (pi0 = [1.0, 0.0]), one step forward simply reads off state 0's row of P, giving pi1 = [0.9, 0.1]. The second step combines both of P's rows, weighted by how likely each state was after step 1: 90% weight on row 0 ([0.9, 0.1]) and 10% weight on row 1 ([0.5, 0.5]), giving pi2 = 0.9*[0.9, 0.1] + 0.1*[0.5, 0.5] = [0.86, 0.14]. This is exactly the Chapman-Kolmogorov idea in action -- summing over every possible intermediate state the chain could have passed through at step 1 -- and matches what np.linalg.matrix_power(P, 2) applied to pi0 would also produce, just computed one step at a time instead of via a precomputed matrix power.

exercises.prompt: This code builds a transition matrix for a 3-state chain and tries to verify it's valid before simulating from it, but the validation silently passes on a broken matrix, and simulation later crashes. Find the bug and fix it.

import numpy as np

P = np.array([
    [0.5, 0.3, 0.1],   # BUG: this row sums to 0.9, not 1.0
    [0.2, 0.5, 0.3],
    [0.1, 0.2, 0.7],
])

def is_valid_transition_matrix(P):
    return (P >= 0).all()   # BUG: only checks non-negativity, never checks row sums

print("valid:", is_valid_transition_matrix(P))

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
current = rng.choice(3, p=P[0])  # raises an error: probabilities do not sum to 1
hints: A valid transition matrix needs every row to be a genuine probability distribution -- non-negative AND summing to exactly 1. The validation function only checks one of those two conditions.
Print P.sum(axis=1) to see which row is the problem -- one of them doesn't add up to 1.0.
Fix the validation function to also check that every row sums to 1 (within floating-point tolerance), and fix the broken row's values so they actually sum to 1.0.
exercises.solutionCode:
import numpy as np

P = np.array([
    [0.5, 0.3, 0.2],   # FIXED: now sums to 1.0
    [0.2, 0.5, 0.3],
    [0.1, 0.2, 0.7],
])

def is_valid_transition_matrix(P, tol=1e-9):
    non_negative = (P >= 0).all()
    rows_sum_to_one = np.allclose(P.sum(axis=1), 1.0, atol=tol)
    return non_negative and rows_sum_to_one

print("valid:", is_valid_transition_matrix(P))

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
current = rng.choice(3, p=P[0])  # now works correctly
print("sampled next state:", current)
exercises.solutionExplanation: A transition matrix's validity requires two separate conditions -- every entry non-negative, AND every row summing to exactly 1 -- because each row is meant to be a complete probability distribution over 'where does the chain go next.' The original `is_valid_transition_matrix` only checked non-negativity, so it happily returned True for a matrix whose first row summed to only 0.9, silently leaving 10% of probability mass unaccounted for. This went undetected until `rng.choice(3, p=P[0])` was called downstream, which requires its `p` argument to sum to exactly 1 and raises an error otherwise. The fix adds the missing row-sum check (using `np.allclose` rather than exact equality, to tolerate floating-point rounding) and corrects the broken row's third value from 0.1 to 0.2 so it genuinely sums to 1.0.

assessments.prompt: Which statement most precisely captures the Markov property?
options: The process has no memory of anything before the current time step, and no amount of state engineering can change that.

Given the current state, the probability distribution over the next state does not depend on any additional information about the states visited before the current one -- the future is conditionally independent of the past given the present.
Every state must have exactly the same probability of transitioning to every other state.
The process must have a finite number of possible states, or the Markov property does not apply.
assessments.explanation: This is the precise statement: conditioning on the current state makes the past irrelevant to predicting the future -- the transition rule depends only on the present state, not on the trajectory that led there. Option A overstates the property into an absolute 'no memory at all' claim, which is exactly the misconception this concept corrects -- the current state can itself be engineered to summarize arbitrary history. Option C fabricates a uniform-transition-probability requirement that has nothing to do with the Markov property. Option D is false; the Markov property is commonly discussed for discrete-state chains but the underlying conditional-independence idea extends to continuous-state processes as well.

assessments.prompt: A stationary distribution pi of a Markov chain with transition matrix P satisfies which equation, and what does that equation mean?
options: pi @ P = pi -- if the chain's current state distribution is pi, applying one more transition step leaves the distribution unchanged.
P @ pi = 0 -- the stationary distribution is any vector that the transition matrix maps to the zero vector.
pi = P^(-1) -- the stationary distribution is the matrix inverse of the transition matrix.
sum(pi) = 0 -- the stationary distribution's entries must cancel out to zero.
assessments.explanation: pi @ P = pi is the defining equation of a stationary distribution: it's a fixed point of the one-step transition operation, meaning the distribution over states is unchanged by taking one more step -- which is also why, under irreducibility and aperiodicity, repeatedly applying P (i.e. P^n for large n) converges to a matrix whose rows all equal pi. Option B describes an unrelated null-space condition that isn't how a stationary distribution is defined. Option C is nonsensical here -- pi is a probability vector, not a matrix, and P^(-1) (even where it exists) isn't what defines stationarity. Option D contradicts the basic requirement that a probability distribution's entries sum to 1, not 0.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague building a simple part-of-speech tagger what the Markov property buys you computationally, what specifically 'hidden' means in a Hidden Markov Model, and why understanding these classical models is a useful step before diving into RNNs or transformer-based sequence models.
assessments.modelAnswer: The Markov property says that once you know a sequence's current state, nothing about the specific path that led to that state changes the probabilities of what happens next -- the future only depends on the past through the present state. Computationally, this is enormously valuable: instead of needing to track and condition on an ever-growing history as a sequence gets longer, you only ever need to carry forward a single current state (or, in the forward algorithm, a small vector of probabilities over hidden states) and a fixed transition rule, which is exactly what makes efficient dynamic-programming algorithms like the forward algorithm and Viterbi algorithm possible at all -- without the Markov property, the computation would need to consider exponentially many possible histories instead of a compact running summary. In a Hidden Markov Model built for part-of-speech tagging, the hidden states are the true grammatical tags (noun, verb, and so on) that generated each word, and 'hidden' means those tags are never directly given to the model -- only the sequence of words themselves is observed. A single word can plausibly have been generated by more than one tag (the word 'run' could be a verb or a noun), so recovering the most likely tag sequence requires genuine probabilistic inference that weighs both how likely each tag is to emit the observed word (the emission probabilities) and how likely one tag is to follow another (the transition probabilities), rather than reading tags straight off the words. Understanding Markov chains and HMMs before moving on to RNNs or transformers is valuable precisely because they make this hidden-state-plus-transition-rule idea fully explicit and small enough to compute and reason about by hand -- an RNN's hidden state, and later, attention over a full sequence, are direct, much more flexible generalizations of exactly this same underlying pattern: keep a compact summary of everything relevant seen so far, update it one step at a time as new input arrives, and use it to explain or predict the next observation.
